questions.q: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle4,3\rangle,\langle2,5\rangle$.
Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle-2,1\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$.
Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle1,2,3\rangle,\langle0,1,4\rangle,\langle5,6,0\rangle$ by cofactor expansion along the first row.
questions.answer: $1\det(\langle1,4\rangle,\langle6,0\rangle)-2\det(\langle0,4\rangle,\langle5,0\rangle)+3\det(\langle0,1\rangle,\langle5,6\rangle) = 1(0-24)-2(0-20)+3(0-5) = -24+40-15=1$.

questions.q: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle2,0,1\rangle,\langle3,1,0\rangle,\langle1,2,4\rangle$ by cofactor expansion along the first row.
questions.answer: $2\det(\langle1,0\rangle,\langle2,4\rangle)-0\det(\langle3,0\rangle,\langle1,4\rangle)+1\det(\langle3,1\rangle,\langle1,2\rangle) = 2(4-0)-0+1(6-1) = 8+5=13$.

questions.q: Recompute the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle1,2,3\rangle,\langle0,1,4\rangle,\langle5,6,0\rangle$ by expanding along the SECOND row instead, to confirm the answer matches.
questions.answer: Expanding along row 2 (with alternating signs $-,+,-$): $-0\det(\langle2,3\rangle,\langle6,0\rangle)+1\det(\langle1,3\rangle,\langle5,0\rangle)-4\det(\langle1,2\rangle,\langle5,6\rangle) = 0+1(0-15)-4(6-10) = -15+16=1$. Matches the earlier result of $1$.

questions.q: For $A$ with rows $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$ and $B$ with rows $\langle2,1\rangle,\langle0,3\rangle$, verify $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$.
questions.answer: $\det A=4-6=-2$, $\det B=6-0=6$, so $\det A\det B=-12$. $AB$ has rows $\langle2,7\rangle,\langle6,15\rangle$ (computed as usual matrix multiplication), and $\det(AB)=2(15)-7(6)=30-42=-12$. They match.

questions.q: Using the product rule $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$, explain why $\det(A^{-1})=\dfrac{1}{\det A}$ for an invertible matrix $A$.
questions.answer: Since $AA^{-1}=I$ and $\det I=1$, the product rule gives $\det(A)\det(A^{-1})=1$. Dividing both sides by $\det A$ (nonzero since $A$ is invertible) gives $\det(A^{-1})=\dfrac{1}{\det A}$.

sections.heading: Determinants and scalar multiples / row operations

questions.q: If $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix with $\det A=5$, find $\det(2A)$ (scaling EVERY entry of $A$ by $2$).
questions.answer: For an $n\times n$ matrix, $\det(cA)=c^n\det A$. For $n=2$: $\det(2A)=2^2(5)=20$.

questions.q: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix with $\det A=5$, find $\det(2A)$.
questions.answer: $\det(2A)=2^3(5)=40$ (note this is different from the $2\times2$ case — the exponent depends on the matrix's size).

questions.q: Swapping two rows of a matrix negates its determinant. If $A$ has rows $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$ with $\det A=-2$, find the determinant of the matrix with rows swapped: $\langle3,4\rangle,\langle1,2\rangle$.
questions.answer: Swapping rows negates the determinant: $\det=-(-2)=2$. (Direct check: $3(2)-4(1)=6-4=2$.)

questions.q: State the invertibility criterion in terms of the determinant.
questions.answer: A square matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det A\ne0$.

questions.q: Is the matrix with rows $\langle2,4\rangle,\langle1,2\rangle$ invertible? Justify using the determinant.
questions.answer: $\det=2(2)-4(1)=0$. Since the determinant is $0$, the matrix is NOT invertible (singular).

questions.q: Is the matrix with rows $\langle1,0,2\rangle,\langle0,3,1\rangle,\langle2,0,4\rangle$ invertible? Justify using the determinant.
questions.answer: Expanding along column 2 (only one nonzero entry, $3$, in position row 2): $\det = -0(\ldots)+3\det(\langle1,2\rangle,\langle2,4\rangle)-0(\ldots) = 3(4-4)=0$. Since $\det=0$, the matrix is NOT invertible.

questions.q: For what value(s) of $k$ is the matrix with rows $\langle k,2\rangle,\langle3,k\rangle$ NOT invertible?
questions.answer: $\det=k^2-6$. Setting $k^2-6=0$ gives $k=\pm\sqrt{6}$. The matrix fails to be invertible exactly when $k=\sqrt{6}$ or $k=-\sqrt{6}$.

questions.q: For what value(s) of $k$ is the matrix with rows $\langle1,k\rangle,\langle k,4\rangle$ NOT invertible?
questions.answer: $\det=4-k^2$. Setting $4-k^2=0$ gives $k=\pm2$. The matrix is singular exactly when $k=2$ or $k=-2$.

questions.q: For a $2\times2$ matrix $A$ with rows $\mathbf{r}_1,\mathbf{r}_2$, $|\det A|$ gives the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$. Find this area for $\mathbf{r}_1=\langle3,0\rangle$, $\mathbf{r}_2=\langle1,4\rangle$.
Explain, using the geometric meaning of the determinant, why a matrix with two identical rows always has determinant $0$.
questions.answer: Two identical rows span a degenerate "parallelogram" with zero area (the two vectors are parallel, in fact equal, so they don't sweep out any two-dimensional region) — matching $\det=0$.

questions.q: Find the determinant of the identity matrix $I_3$ (rows $\langle1,0,0\rangle,\langle0,1,0\rangle,\langle0,0,1\rangle$).
questions.answer: $\det I_3=1$ (expanding along any row/column, the product of the diagonal entries, all $1$'s, with every off-diagonal cofactor contributing $0$).

questions.q: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle3,0,0\rangle,\langle0,-2,0\rangle,\langle0,0,5\rangle$ (a diagonal matrix).
questions.answer: For a diagonal (or more generally triangular) matrix, the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: $3(-2)(5)=-30$.

questions.q: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle0,0,3\rangle,\langle0,1,0\rangle,\langle3,0,0\rangle$, and explain why it is nonzero even though the main diagonal has two zeros.
questions.answer: Expanding along row 2 (only nonzero entry is the middle $1$): $\det=1\cdot\det(\langle0,3\rangle,\langle3,0\rangle)=1(0-9)=-9$. The main-diagonal shortcut only applies to TRIANGULAR matrices; this matrix is not triangular (it has nonzero entries above AND below the diagonal), so the diagonal-product rule doesn't apply here.

questions.q: Find the determinant of the zero matrix (all entries $0$) of any size, and connect this to the invertibility criterion.
questions.answer: $\det=0$ for the zero matrix of any size (every row is the zero vector, so every cofactor expansion term vanishes). This matches the invertibility criterion: the zero matrix is never invertible.

questions.q: Explain why any matrix with an entire row (or column) of zeros must have determinant $0$, using cofactor expansion along that row.
questions.answer: Expanding along a row of all zeros, every term in the cofactor expansion is (zero entry)$\times$(its cofactor)$=0$, so the whole sum is $0$.

questions.q: Cramer's Rule solves $ax+by=e$, $cx+dy=f$ via $x=\dfrac{\det A_x}{\det A}$, $y=\dfrac{\det A_y}{\det A}$, where $A$ is the coefficient matrix and $A_x,A_y$ replace the respective column with $\langle e,f\rangle$. Use it to solve $2x+3y=8$, $x-y=1$.
questions.answer: $A$ has rows $\langle2,3\rangle,\langle1,-1\rangle$, $\det A=-2-3=-5$. $A_x$ has rows $\langle8,3\rangle,\langle1,-1\rangle$, $\det A_x=-8-3=-11$, so $x=\dfrac{-11}{-5}=\dfrac{11}{5}$. $A_y$ has rows $\langle2,8\rangle,\langle1,1\rangle$, $\det A_y=2-8=-6$, so $y=\dfrac{-6}{-5}=\dfrac{6}{5}$.

questions.q: Explain why Cramer's Rule fails (gives no unique solution) whenever $\det A=0$.
questions.answer: Division by $\det A=0$ is undefined, and this matches the invertibility criterion: $\det A=0$ means the coefficient matrix is singular, so the system does not have a unique solution (it has either no solution or infinitely many).

questions.q: Compare Cramer's Rule to Gaussian elimination as a solution method for large systems (say, $10$ equations in $10$ unknowns). Which is more practical, and why?
questions.answer: Gaussian elimination is far more practical for large systems: it requires roughly $O(n^3)$ operations, while Cramer's Rule requires computing $n+1$ separate $n\times n$ determinants, each costing far more via cofactor expansion — Cramer's Rule is mainly useful for small systems ($2\times2$ or $3\times3$) or for theoretical formulas, not large-scale computation.
